    Practitioners — Africa — Therapists¶

    Jurisdictional context¶

    Africa is a regional aggregate; deepening per-country (especially South Africa) is pending and the file should be read as a regional placeholder anchored by South Africa with institutional / feminist-legal entries elsewhere. South Africa is the only African jurisdiction with a verifiable, named-on-record clinical PA practitioner cluster. The statutory frame is the Children's Act 38/2005 (best-interests-of-the-child paramount), the Maintenance Act 99/1998, and the Supreme Court of Appeal / High Court family-law line that has crystallised PA as a clinically and judicially recognised phenomenon in the leading authority T.L.D v B.G (015642/2022) [2023] ZAGPJHC 801 (Adams J, Gauteng Local Division Johannesburg, 13 July 2023). Clinical psychology is regulated by the Health Professions Council of South Africa (HPCSA) Professional Board for Psychology (clinical / counselling / educational / forensic categories); social work is regulated by the SA Council for Social Service Professions (SACSSP) under the Social Service Professions Act 110/1978. Parenting coordinators are accredited via NABFAM with voluntary associations FAMAC, KAFAM, SAAM. SA Standards of Practice for Forensic Assessments were drafted in 2021 (Martalas-chaired task force).

    The rest of the continent is institutional / feminist-legal at best. Kenya's Children Act 2022 codifies best-interests-of-the-child as paramount; Kenya's High Court line on custody is developing but no named-on-record PA clinical expert has been located; the Counsellors and Psychologists Board (CPRB) under the Counsellors and Psychologists Act 2014 is the statutory psychology regulator. Nigeria's federal Child Rights Act 2003 has been adopted by 27 of 36 states with state-level variation; the Matrimonial Causes Act provides the divorce-side framework; the Nigeria Association of Clinical Psychologists (NACP) is the professional body but has issued no public PA position. Egypt's Personal Status Law (with 2004 Family Courts Law 10) and the family-court structure govern custody / hadana decisions; the National Council for Childhood and Motherhood (NCCM, Presidential Decree 54/1988) is the statutory child-rights body. The African critique register is carried not by clinicians but by women's-rights NGOs — in South Africa Mosaic and Women Watch SA; in Kenya FIDA Kenya (the Federation of Women Lawyers); in Nigeria Project Alert on Violence Against Women and Women's Aid Collective (WACOL). Peer-reviewed African PA literature is thin: outside the SA cluster (Viljoen 2014; Bosch-Brits, Wessels & Roux 2018) there is no substantive African journal output on PA.

    Structural findings¶

    • Africa is anchored by South Africa only at the clinical level. SA is the sole African jurisdiction with named-on-record PA clinicians (Carr, Roux, Olivier, Els, Martalas, Viljoen, NWU social-work team) verifiable via a leading apex judgment (T.L.D v B.G [2023] ZAGPJHC 801). This centrality is recognition for SA, not an evaluative ranking — other African jurisdictions simply have no clinical-level PA practitioner record to verify within public primary sources.
    • Other African jurisdictions surface only at institutional or feminist-legal collective level. Kenya: CPRB (regulator) + FIDA Kenya (feminist-legal critique register). Nigeria: NACP (association) + Project Alert + WACOL (feminist-legal critique register). Egypt: NCCM (statutory child-rights body, middle / critique-leaning per 2016 personal-status-reform position). Zero named individual PA clinicians located in KE / NG / EG / GH / TZ / ZW / UG / BW / MA within time-budget public-web search.
    • Peer-reviewed African PA literature is thin and SA-monopolised. Viljoen & van Rensburg (J. Divorce & Remarriage 2014) and Bosch-Brits, Wessels & Roux (Social Work / Maatskaplike Werk 2018 SciELO) are the only African peer-reviewed PA-engaging studies located. No PA-position statement comparable to CFP Brazil NT 4/2022 or COLPSIC Colombia 2023 located from HPCSA, SACSSP, CPRB, NACP, NPA, EPA or NCCM.
    • The African critique register is institutional and women's-rights-organisation-led, not clinician-led — mirroring the India pattern. SA: Mosaic + Women Watch SA. Kenya: FIDA Kenya. Nigeria: Project Alert + WACOL. Egypt: NCCM's 2016 personal-status-reform opposition is the closest institutional-critique signal. No African clinician carries a published PA-critique line comparable to Germany (Zimmermann / Fichtner / Walper) or Spain (Vaccaro).
    • Regulator-silence is the second load-bearing structural finding. HPCSA Professional Board for Psychology and SACSSP have issued no PA-position notice; CPRB Kenya, NACP Nigeria, and the Egyptian Psychiatric Association are likewise institutionally silent on PA. This regulator-silence parallels the IPS / IACP pattern in India and the Netherlands document-led pattern, but the SA institutional anchor carrying positional weight is the High Court (T.L.D v B.G) rather than the regulator.
    • September 2026 Sub-Saharan expansion: 12 entries added — Ghana 3 (Psychology Council, Department of Social Welfare and Development, Domestic Violence Secretariat), Nigeria 1 (Nigeria Association of Social Workers), Kenya 2 (Dr Jane Wanjao, State Department for Children Services), Uganda 1 (National Children Authority), Tanzania 1 (Department of Social Welfare), Ethiopia 1 (Ministry of Women and Social Affairs), Zimbabwe 1 (Allied Health Practitioners Council), Namibia 2 (Social Work and Psychology Board, Legal Assistance Centre). The file now holds 33 entries: critique 5, forensic-evaluator 1, institutional 17, middle 3, recognition 7. Eleven of the twelve are institutional, which extends rather than breaks the regulator-silence finding above: none of these bodies publishes any position on parental alienation, and that silence is recorded as the finding rather than inferred as a stance. Dr Jane Wanjao (Nairobi) is the first named non-South-African clinician in this file to meet the directory standard, on a 2023 Pan Africa Christian University doctorate and an AJOL-indexed article; her Counsellors and Psychologists Board registration could NOT be confirmed, because the Kenyan CPB portal exposes no public register search. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: web search was unavailable for two of the three research passes behind this batch, so the absence of named clinicians in Nigeria, Ghana, Ethiopia, Zimbabwe and Namibia is a tooling limitation, not evidence of absence, and those jurisdictions should be re-run before the gap is treated as settled. The Tanzanian entry quotes Swahili-only sources in the researcher's own working translation, which a Swahili reader should confirm.

    Recognition camp¶

    Leonard Carr¶

    Clinical Psychologist; UNISA-trained; 40+ years' clinical practice; HPCSA Professional Board for Psychology (Clinical) registration + Board of Health Funders (BHF) Johannesburg · Gauteng (Norwood / Parkwood) · Independent clinical psychology private practice (Life on Iris, Norwood, Johannesburg); medico-legal and forensic-psychology consulting; clinical psychologist of record in T.L.D v B.G [2023] ZAGPJHC 801 (final report 10 March 2023 adopted by Adams J)

    Stance: Court-appointed clinical psychologist whose final report drove South Africa's leading 2023 PA judgment. In T.L.D v B.G [2023] ZAGPJHC 801 (Adams J, GLD Johannesburg, 13 July 2023) Carr's final report of 10 March 2023 found the child susceptible to 'clinging onto the most actively influencing and persuasive parent's belief system' and that PA made the child's world 'treacherous and emotionally dangerous'; recommended three months protective separation; curator ad litem Adv Mark Haskins SC agreed with all findings. Father's contact suspended for three months on PA findings; primary residence/parental rights to mother. Single highest-leverage SA recognition-camp clinical interlocutor at apex-of-record level.

    Publications: - Court-adopted PA assessment in T.L.D v B.G (015642/2022) [2023] ZAGPJHC 801 — final report 10 March 2023 (2023) — Gauteng Local Division Johannesburg (Adams J); SAFLII — https://www.saflii.org/za/cases/ZAGPJHC/2023/801.html - Psychology of Shalom / Harmony framework — practice portfolio (2020) — leonardcarr.com practice site

    Clinical Psychologist (HPCSA Professional Board for Psychology) since 1986 (37+ yrs); PhD Child and Forensic Psychology; NABFAM accredited Parenting Coordinator + Family Law Mediator; SAMLA accredited Medico-Legal Practitioner Benoni and Cape Town (dual-practice) · Gauteng + Western Cape · Independent clinical psychology private practice (Benoni + Cape Town); psycho-legal and forensic assessments; mediation, restorative justice, collaborative law; parenting coordinator of record in T.L.D v B.G; NABFAM Chairperson (per De Rebus Aug 2018)

    Christie Els¶

    Counselling Psychologist (HPCSA Professional Board for Psychology); MA Psychology, University of the Free State (UFS); Board of Health Funders (BHF); 24+ years' private practice; Family Bridges Program-trained (USA, April 2014); first South African included in international Parental Alienation Study Group (PASG), March 2015 George · Western Cape (Garden Route, Heather Park) · Independent counselling psychology private practice (Heather Park, George); father's expert of record in T.L.D v B.G [2023] ZAGPJHC 801

    Stance: Named father's expert in T.L.D v B.G [2023] ZAGPJHC 801 per Bregman Moodley summary. Acacia Training speaker bio: 'the first South African to be included in the international Parental Alienation Study Group, a selected group of mental health and law professionals from 32 countries'; LinkedIn: Family Bridges Program training April 2014, PASG inclusion March 2015. Most-credentialled SA recognition-camp PA / reunification clinician. CAVEAT: ACTIVE HPCSA DISCIPLINARY PROCESS as at MedicalBrief 1 May 2024 — Eastern Circuit Local Division (Thembalethu, George) Patrick Gamble J dismissed Els's application to stop HPCSA disciplinary action, describing her conduct as 'vexatious' and 'Stalingrad'-style stalling; preliminary investigation found her guilty of misconduct (R50,000 admission-of-guilt fine offered) for allegedly operating outside her mandate as court-appointed facilitator (Els v HPCSA and Others (5845/2022) [2022] ZAWCHC 106, 30 May 2022). High media-sensitivity entry — outreach must acknowledge regulatory exposure honestly.

    Dr Marlé Viljoen¶

    Clinical Psychologist (HPCSA Professional Board for Psychology); MA Clinical Psychology, North-West University (NWU) 2014 Centurion · Gauteng · Independent clinical psychology private practice (Centurion); peer-reviewed PA author

    Stance: Viljoen, M. & van Rensburg, E., 'Exploring the lived experience of psychologists working with parental alienation syndrome', Journal of Divorce and Remarriage 55(4):253-275 (2014) — standard SA peer-reviewed citation on PA-syndrome clinical practice. Viljoen MA dissertation (NWU, 2014) 'Exploring the lived experiences of psychologists working with Parental Alienation Syndrome'. Viljoen defines PA as 'a set of processes and behaviours conducted and enacted by a parent to deliberately and knowingly damage or sever the relationship between a child and another parent with whom the child enjoyed a prior loving relationship' — quoted in De Rebus August 2018 and divorcelaws.co.za. The natural recognition-camp Gauteng peer-reviewed citation in every SA practitioner long-form on PA. Surname romanisation varies (Marlé / Marile / Marilé) across sources — J. Divorce & Remarriage byline is authoritative form.

    Publications: - Exploring the lived experience of psychologists working with parental alienation syndrome (Viljoen & van Rensburg) (2014) — Journal of Divorce and Remarriage 55(4):253-275 - MA dissertation: Exploring the lived experiences of psychologists working with Parental Alienation Syndrome (2014) — North-West University (NWU) - De Rebus August 2018 PA article (Viljoen quoted alongside Roux) (2018) — De Rebus — http://www.derebus.org.za/parental-alienation-can-be-overcome/

    Elsabé Bosch-Brits + Prof Cornelia Wessels + Dr Adrie Roux (NWU social-work team)¶

    Bosch-Brits — Social Worker in Private Practice (study lead, SACSSP-registered); Wessels — Professor, School of Psychosocial Behavioural Sciences, Social Work Division, NWU Potchefstroom Campus; Roux — Dr / Senior Lecturer, same Division Potchefstroom (NWU) · North-West Province · North-West University (NWU) Social Work Division, Potchefstroom Campus; Bosch-Brits private practice

    Stance: Bosch-Brits, E., Wessels, C. & Roux, A., 'Fathers' Experience and Perceptions of Parent Alienation in High-Conflict Divorce', Social Work / Maatskaplike Werk 54(1) (2018) — SciELO peer-reviewed qualitative study identifying eight themes (intense hurt 'worse than death'; unparalleled anger; loss of self-worth; distrust of women; loss of parental rights; constant concern; distrust of legal system; supervised contact trauma); notes PA observed in SA practice but remains under-utilised terminology in SA courts and not formally addressed as an urgent problem despite 28% rise in divorces 2012-2013. SACSSP-side peer-reviewed qualitative anchor on fathers' lived experience of PA in SA — standard SA citation when recognition-camp argument needs an SA social-work journal (not psychology) reference.

    Dr Jane Njango Wanjao¶

    PhD Marriage and Family Therapy, Pan Africa Christian University (dissertation submitted June 2023 — verified from dissertation title page); MA Counselling Psychology, Daystar University (stated on practitioner-directory profiles, not verified against a university record); described on directory profiles as a Licensed Marriage and Family Therapist Nairobi · Nairobi County, Kenya · SID Counselling Centre, Nairobi (practice named on TherapyRoute profile); doctoral graduate of Pan Africa Christian University, supervised by Dr Margaret Njoroge (Department of Psychology, United States International University) and Dr Elizabeth Kamau (Department of Psychology, Pan Africa Christian University) per the dissertation front matter

    Stance: Wanjao's doctoral dissertation (Pan Africa Christian University, June 2023) adopts, in its Definition of Terms, Warshak's (2020) definition of parental alienation as 'The manipulation of children by one parent with an intention of turning them against the other parent after divorce', adding that 'In this study parental alienation will be taken to mean post-divorce parental alienation'. Her own abstract states that 'post-divorce parental alienation creates an unfavourable environment which may derange the adolescents from thriving' and that 'PDPA harms the cognitive, social and behavioural domains of most adolescents and this threatens their wellbeing'. The study reports a statistically significant relationship between post-divorce parental alienation and adolescents' interpersonal relationships, sense of accomplishment and meaning, and recommends awareness-raising on collaborative parenting plus 'coordination of key stake holders like children attorneys, marriage and family therapists as well as the ministry of education'. Stance recorded as recognition strictly on the basis of this published framing of parental alienation as a harmful post-divorce phenomenon; no forensic, court-appointed or expert-witness role is claimed in, or documented by, any source opened.

    Publications: - Relationship between Parental Alienation and Interpersonal Relationships: A case of adolescents' in selected high schools in Kiambu County, Kenya (Wanjao, Njoroge & Kamau) (2023) — African Journal of Education, Science and Technology 7(3):266-274 (AJOL-indexed) — https://www.ajol.info/index.php/ajedscitech/article/view/254458 - Relationship Between Post-Divorce Parental Alienation and Adolescents' Wellbeing in Public Mixed Day High Schools in Kikuyu Sub County, Kenya (PhD dissertation) (2023) — Pan Africa Christian University, Graduate School — PhD Marriage and Family Therapy — https://repository.pacuniversity.ac.ke/bitstreams/b9a3ed14-d410-4208-9360-7fc52ebbbaba/download - Practice-blog presentation of the post-divorce parental alienation study (2024) — SID Counselling (practice blog), post dated 5 November 2024 — https://sidcounselling.com/relationship-between-post-divorce-parental-alienation-and-adolescents-wellbeing-in/

    Dr Astrid Martalas¶

    Counselling Psychologist (HPCSA Professional Board for Psychology); MA Counselling Psychology Stellenbosch 1999; PhD parenting coordination University of Utrecht (Netherlands) 2018; FAMAC accredited mediator 2005 + parenting coordinator/facilitator 2008; NABFAM Cape Town · Western Cape (Green Point) · Pomegranate (parenting coordination, mediation, child/adolescent psychology, parenting/contact/care/relocation assessments); court-appointed parenting coordinator and/or mediator in 300+ matters; chair 2021 task force that drafted SA Standards of Practice for Forensic Assessments; member 2016 task force that drafted SA Parenting Coordination Guidelines; FAMAC executive since 2006 (twice co-chair); NABFAM vice-chair (elected 2018)

    Stance: Pomegranate practice page: 'the resolution of family disputes through parenting co-ordination … court appointed as parenting coordinator and/or mediator in more than 300 matters'. Published frame is parenting-coordination / child-participation / dispute-resolution (Martalas, paper on child participation, University of Leiden 2014 in 'The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child: Taking Stock After 25 Years'; Martalas, 'Dispute resolution in South Africa: parenting coordination keeps families out of court', International Family Law Conference 2016; AFCC presentations New Orleans 2015, Melbourne 2017, Sydney 2019) rather than PA-syndrome recognition or PA-critique. Stance middle because published frame is procedural / forensic-standards rather than partisan PA position; PA-specific public statement not publicly confirmed. Most-institutionally-embedded SA parenting-coordination clinician — natural middle-camp procedural interlocutor for any PA matter requiring forensic-assessment-standards compliance.

    Statutory child-rights and family-policy body established by Presidential Decree 54/1988; formulates, coordinates, monitors and evaluates policy for protection and development of children and mothers in Egypt; operates Child Helpline 16000 and Child Rescue Department psychological-support / family-counselling unit; Safe Child Unit pilot across six governorates announced January 2026 Cairo · Egypt national · Statutory state body under Presidential Decree 54/1988

    Stance: NCCM policy frame combines (a) psychological support, family counselling, behaviour modification, and speech therapy via Child Rescue Department + Helpline 16000 (66,645 calls Jan-Feb 2025; 3,457 complaints / assistance requests addressed) and (b) NCCM's 2016 public position (per Mada Masr 28 Dec 2016) opposing draft personal-status reforms that would have expanded non-custodial parent access on women-safety grounds — placing NCCM in middle / critique-leaning position on PA-adjacent custody-access reform under Egyptian Personal Status Law and Family Courts Law 10/2004. Specific direct PA-position notice not publicly confirmed. Egypt's standing statutory child-rights / family-policy body and state operator of Child Helpline psychological-support unit — only institutional Egyptian addressee with both a public stance on PA-adjacent custody-access reform (critique-leaning per 2016 Mada Masr) and operational psychological-support capacity.     Forensic evaluators¶

    Dr de Wit¶

    Dr (title as cited in judgment; specific HPCSA category and registration number not publicly disclosed in the judgment text) Johannesburg · Gauteng · Independent expert engaged in T.L.D v B.G [2023] ZAGPJHC 801 (no institutional affiliation disclosed in the public judgment record)

    Stance: Court-engaged expert in T.L.D v B.G (015642/2022) [2023] ZAGPJHC 801 (Adams J, 13 July 2023). Per the judgment as summarised in primary South African family-law coverage, Dr de Wit assessed the father's personality dynamics and found that his behaviour was driven by pathological envy characterised as 'spoiling hostility' aimed at devastating the other parent, alongside narcissism and a sense of entitlement — a finding the court relied upon together with Mr Leonard Carr's child evaluation in ordering protective separation. This places De Wit as a forensic evaluator whose findings supported a recognition/protection outcome in a landmark SA parental-alienation judgment.

    Verification: - https://www.saflii.org/za/cases/ZAGPJHC/2023/801.html - https://familylaws.co.za/parental-alienation-syndrome-landmark-case-south-africa/ - https://familylaws.co.za/parental-alienation-south-africa-family-law/

    Contact: Not publicly confirmed

    Notes: Verified existence and forensic role via the SAFLII case citation and two independent primary-source South African family-law analyses of T.L.D v B.G [2023] ZAGPJHC 801 which both quote De Wit's findings on paternal narcissism / pathological envy. First name, HPCSA registration number, institutional affiliation and current practice address are NOT disclosed in the public judgment record or in any publicly indexed HPCSA / university / clinic page located within the search budget. Entry is recovered as a named expert in the case record but must remain narrowly scoped until HPCSA register direct-query (manual) or court transcript yields fuller identity.

    National professional body for clinical psychologists in Nigeria; federal licensing under Nigerian Psychological Association / Federal Ministry of Health Federal (national) · Nigeria national · NACP — national professional association

    Stance: No public PA-position notice located for NACP / NPA within time-budget search. Family-court PA jurisprudence in Nigeria operates under Matrimonial Causes Act + Child Rights Act 2003 (federal, adopted by 27 of 36 states with state-level variation) with best-interests-of-the-child as paramount (per Chancery, Strand & Lyon Associates legal opinion). FIDA Nigeria + Project Alert + WACOL carry the women-lawyer / DV-protective critique register cross-referenced under entries below. Nigeria's institutional clinical-psychology body — natural addressee for any Nigeria-side PA-training submission. No named Nigerian clinical-psychologist PA practitioner located within time-budget public-web search. Honest gap acknowledged.

    Psychology Council, Ghana (Ghana Psychology Council)¶

    Statutory regulator of the psychology profession in Ghana under Part 5 of the Health Professions Regulatory Bodies Act, 2013 (Act 857); registers and licenses Professional Psychologists, Psychologist Assistants, Paraprofessionals and Lay Practitioners; accredits applied-psychology programmes of study; publishes the official Gazette register of licensed practitioners Accra (Legon) · Ghana national · Statutory body established under the Health Professions Regulatory Bodies Act, 2013 (Act 857); works with the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission on programme accreditation

    Stance: The Council's own site states it 'is the only Regulatory Body mandated by the Health Professions Act 857, Section 5 to register and license all persons who have been trained in Psychology and Applied Psychology to enable them practice legally in Ghana', and describes itself as 'An independent statutory body protecting the Ghanaian public by accrediting programmes, licensing practitioners and enforcing the highest standards of professional practice.' Its published mandate is confined to training standards, accreditation, registration, licensing and renewal; no position statement, guideline or notice on parental alienation, resist-refuse dynamics or post-separation child contact appears anywhere in the site's page inventory as inspected. It is listed here as Ghana's registry of record — the body against which the credentials of any Ghana-based psychology expert giving evidence in a custody or contact matter should be checked — and as a documented instance of regulator silence on the parental-alienation construct, the same pattern already recorded for CPRB Kenya, NACP Nigeria, HPCSA and SACSSP. Classified institutional per schema as a statutory regulator.

    Publications: - Establishment and regulatory mandate under Part 5 of the Health Professions Regulatory Bodies Act, 2013 (Act 857) (2013) — Parliament of Ghana; cited on the Council's About page — https://ghanapsychologycouncil.gov.gh/about.html - Extraordinary Gazette No. 97 — official public register of individuals licensed to practise psychology, counselling and applied psychology in Ghana (2026) — Psychology Council, Ghana (Gazetted Members page) — https://ghanapsychologycouncil.gov.gh/gazetted-members.html - Licensing and registration categories: Professional Psychologist, Psychologist Assistant, Paraprofessional, Lay Practitioner (2026) — Psychology Council, Ghana — https://ghanapsychologycouncil.gov.gh/licensing-registration.html

The Gazetted Members page links a register PDF (Extraordinary Gazette No. 97, March 2026); the link was confirmed live (HTTP 200, content-type application/pdf, 1,563,454 bytes) but the PDF contents were not parsed, so no individual registrant was checked against it. 'Anna Plange' is shown on the site as Acting Registrar; that title is time-sensitive and is therefore not asserted in the entry body. No registration number is recorded because the Council is the registering body rather than a registrant.

    Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), Ghana¶

    Government statutory agency under the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection; first established 1946 by Local Ordinance Order No. 66 (as the Department of Social Welfare and Housing), becoming the Department of Social Welfare in 1950; operates a Child and Family Welfare Division and a Justice Administration Division (Probation, Correctional, Aftercare and Community Service Units) Accra · Ghana national (implementing functions decentralised to district assemblies since 2011) · Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection (MoGCSP), Republic of Ghana

    Stance: The Department's published mandate is 'to take the lead role in integrating the disadvantaged, vulnerable, persons with disabilities and the excluded into mainstream society', and its stated regulatory framework expressly includes the Children's Act 1998 (Act 560), the Children's (Amendment) Act 937 of 2016, the Juvenile Justice Act 2003 (Act 653), the Domestic Violence Act (Act 732) and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. Its Child and Family Welfare Division is tasked to 'Design child and family welfare programmes and activities to effectively prevent and protect children from all forms of violence, abuse, neglect and exploitation', to 'Empower children and families to better understand abusive situations and make choices to prevent and respond to situations of risk', and to 'Provide alternative care for children without parental care'; its Justice Administration Division states it 'Assists the court in cases involving juveniles' through a Probation Unit. The Department is therefore Ghana's statutory child-and-family-welfare arm and the social-work interface with the courts, and is the natural institutional addressee for any Ghana-side proposal on post-separation contact practice. No reference to parental alienation, resist-refuse dynamics, custody or access disputes, or social enquiry reports in contact proceedings appears in the Department's published functions as inspected; classified institutional per schema.

    Publications: - Departmental mandate and regulatory framework citing the Children's Act 1998 (Act 560) among its governing statutes (1998) — Parliament of Ghana; listed on the Department of Social Welfare page, MoGCSP — https://www.mogcsp.gov.gh/department-of-social-welfare/ - Children's (Amendment) Act 937, cited in the Department's regulatory framework (2016) — Parliament of Ghana; listed on the Department of Social Welfare page, MoGCSP — https://www.mogcsp.gov.gh/department-of-social-welfare/ - Child and Family Welfare Division and Justice Administration Division functions (child protection, alternative care, probation, assistance to the court) (2026) — Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, Ghana — https://www.mogcsp.gov.gh/department-of-social-welfare/

    Verification: - https://www.mogcsp.gov.gh/ - https://www.mogcsp.gov.gh/department-of-social-welfare/ - https://www.mogcsp.gov.gh/about/departments/ - https://www.mogcsp.gov.gh/school-of-social-work-osu/

    Contact: P.O. Box MBO 186, Ministries, Accra; info@mogcsp.gov.gh; (+233) 0302 688181/7/4; (+233) 0302 688188; https://www.mogcsp.gov.gh/department-of-social-welfare/

The task brief's framing of Family Tribunals and social enquiry reports could NOT be confirmed from the Department's own published pages — neither Family Tribunals, custody, access, maintenance nor social enquiry reports are mentioned there — and no such role is asserted in this entry.     Domestic Violence Secretariat (DVS), Ghana¶

    Statutory secretariat established by the Domestic Violence Act, 2007 (Act 732); managed by a thirteen-member Management Board established under that Act; sits under the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection Accra · Ghana national · Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection (MoGCSP), Republic of Ghana

    Stance: The Secretariat's own page states it 'was established by Domestic Violence Act, 2007 Act 732' and that 'The mandate of the Domestic Violence Secretariat is to provide protection against domestic violence particularly for women and children', with the overall goal of facilitating 'the elimination of domestic violence from the Ghanaian Society, create family cohesion and provide for a peaceful environment for national development'. Its listed functions include setting standards of practice informing intra-agency and interagency protocols, acting as central depository for domestic-violence information, facilitating state-run shelters and standards for private shelters, and setting up complaints mechanisms for survivors. It is recorded here as Ghana's statutory domestic-violence body — the institutional counterpart on the safeguarding side of any post-separation contact question, structurally parallel to the women's-rights and DV-protective entries already held for Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa, but distinguished from them by being a state body rather than an NGO. No published position on parental alienation or on contested-contact proceedings was located; classified institutional per schema rather than critique, because no critique of the parental-alienation construct appears in its own documents.

    Publications: - Establishment and mandate under the Domestic Violence Act, 2007 (Act 732) (2007) — Parliament of Ghana; cited on the Domestic Violence Secretariat page, MoGCSP — https://www.mogcsp.gov.gh/domestic-violence-secretariat-dv/ - Core functions: standards of practice, interagency protocols, central information depository, state-run and private shelter standards, survivor complaints mechanisms (2017) — Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, Ghana — https://www.mogcsp.gov.gh/domestic-violence-secretariat-dv/

The Domestic Violence Act is cited on that page as 'Domestic Violence Act, 2007 Act 732'.     Nigeria Association of Social Workers (NASoW)¶

    National professional association of social workers in Nigeria; describes itself as the umbrella professional body of all social workers in Nigeria and the only recognised national association for social workers in the country; member organisation of the International Federation of Social Workers (IFSW) Abuja · Federal Capital Territory (members at local, state and federal levels nationwide) · Nigeria Association of Social Workers (NASoW); IFSW member organisation

    Stance: NASoW's own site states it 'is the umbrella professional body of all Social Workers in Nigeria', that it 'works to enhance the professional growth and development of its members, to create and maintain professional standards for Social Workers and to advance sound social policies in the country', and that its members work across schools, teaching hospitals, NGOs, ministries, departments and agencies, rehabilitation centres and correctional centres. IFSW's member-organisation record for Nigeria lists NASoW as established in 1975 and an IFSW member since 1976, with approximately 4,100 members. NASoW has published no position statement on parental alienation or post-separation child contact that could be located.

    Publications: - IFSW member-organisation record for Nigeria (NASoW established 1975; joined IFSW 1976; approx. 4,100 members) (1976) — International Federation of Social Workers — https://www.ifsw.org/member-organisation/nigeria/

    Contact: Area 3, State Social Welfare office, Block B, 1st Floor, office 3, opposite Secondary Education Board, Orlu Street, Abuja, Federal Capital Territory; info@nasow.org; +234 703 7362 210; http://www.nasow.org/

    Notes: Existence, self-description, contact details and the RC number were read directly from the Association's own website (nasow.org, which redirects from https to http://www.nasow.org/). IFSW's own member-organisation page for Nigeria independently confirms NASoW as the Nigerian member body and supplies the 1975 founding year, 1976 IFSW accession and membership figure. NASoW is a professional association, NOT a statutory regulator: no statutory Nigerian social-work regulator or public practitioner register was located within this task's budget, and the RC number is a corporate registration rather than evidence of a licensure register. The two sources disagree on secondary details — IFSW lists the website as www.nasowng.org (which does not resolve from this environment), a different email (nasownigeria1975@gmail.com), a different Abuja address, and a president, Mr Alhaji Mashood Mustapha, who is not named on NASoW's own site; those details are flagged rather than asserted here. Descriptive only: no claim is made that NASoW endorses, opposes or has adopted any position on parental alienation.

    State Department for Children Services (Kenya)¶

    Institutional: Kenyan government state department under the Ministry of Gender, Culture and Children Services; administers the Children Act (Chapter 141, Laws of Kenya); mandate set out in Executive Order No. 1 of 2025 Nairobi · Kenya national · Ministry of Gender, Culture and Children Services; operates 8 regional, 47 County and 407 Sub-County offices, statutory children's institutions and Child Helpline 116

    Stance: The State Department's published mandate page lists, among the mandates contained in Executive Order No. 1 of 2025, the 'Enforcement of children's right to parental care and protection, which includes equal responsibility of the mother and father to provide for the child, whether they are married to each other or not', alongside 'Administration of Family Policy and Family Protection Policies' and 'Administer the Children Act chapter 141, Laws of Kenya)'. Its 'Who We Are' page states the department 'is mandated to safeguard and strengthen families as the foundation of society while promoting the welfare, rights, and social development of children', and lists 'Best interest of the child' and 'Child Participation' among its principle values. This is the Kenyan statutory children's-services apparatus whose county and sub-county children's officers sit behind child-welfare reporting in family proceedings, making it the institutional addressee for any Kenya-side submission on post-separation contact. No parental-alienation-specific position paper, guideline or notice was located on any State Department page opened; the silence is recorded as the finding rather than inferred as a stance.

    National Children Authority (NCA), Uganda¶

    Statutory body established in May 2016 by the Children (Amendment) Act 2016 (Act No. 9 of 2016); hosted under the Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development Kampala · Uganda national · Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development (MGLSD), Gender & Labour House, Kampala; works alongside the MGLSD Department of Youth and Children Affairs

    Stance: The MGLSD page for the National Children Authority records that the Authority was established in May 2016 by the Children (Amendment) Act 2016 No. 9 'to provide a structure and mechanism, which will ensure proper co-ordination, monitoring and evaluation of policies and child rights programs'. Its listed functions include advising Government on the formulation of a National Child Protection Policy, monitoring 'the implementation of laws relating to all forms of child abuse', receiving complaints from the public relating to child abuse, and conducting and co-ordinating research on child abuse; the same page discusses monitoring the functionality of Family and Children Courts (FCCs), which are the Ugandan forum for custody and access matters. This makes the NCA Uganda's statutory child-rights co-ordination body and the institutional addressee for any Uganda-side submission on children's post-separation contact. No parental-alienation-specific position, guideline or statement was located on any NCA or MGLSD page opened, and none is inferred.

    Department of Social Welfare (Idara ya Ustawi wa Jamii), Ministry of Community Development, Gender, Women and Special Groups, Tanzania¶

    Institutional: department of a United Republic of Tanzania ministry (MoCDGWSG / Wizara ya Maendeleo ya Jamii, Jinsia, Wanawake na Makundi Maalum); delivers statutory social-welfare services through Maafisa Ustawi wa Jamii (social welfare officers) at council level; the ministry's Child Development Department cites Sheria ya Mtoto Na. 21 ya Mwaka 2009 (Law of the Child Act No. 21 of 2009, as amended 2019) as its governing law Dodoma · Tanzania national · Ministry of Community Development, Gender, Women and Special Groups (MoCDGWSG), Mji wa Serikali Mtumba, Dodoma; Department of Social Welfare and Child Development Department

    Stance: The department's own page states its principal aim as 'Kutoa huduma za ustawi wa jamii zenye viwango vya usawa, haki, ubora na endelevu kwa wananchi hususan makundi maalum' (to provide social-welfare services of equitable, just, quality and sustainable standard, particularly for special groups), and its second specific objective is 'Kumarisha malezi, matunzo na ulinzi wa Watoto walio katika mazingira hatarishi ikiwa ni pamoja na huduma za malezi ya kambo, uasili na usuluhishi wa ndoa zenye migogoro' — strengthening the upbringing, care and protection of children in vulnerable circumstances, including foster care, adoption and the reconciliation of marriages in conflict. The ministry separately publishes 'Usuluhishi wa Ndoa na Familia' (marriage and family reconciliation) as a listed public service, and lists Maafisa Ustawi wa Jamii (social welfare officers) and wanasaikolojia (psychologists) among the providers of its mental-health and psychosocial support service, which it says responds to 'Migogoro ya ndoa na familia' (marriage and family conflicts) among other stressors. This is therefore the Tanzanian statutory apparatus through which separating families and children's welfare matters are handled administratively. No parental-alienation-specific position, guideline or statement was located on any ministry page opened; parental alienation is not an established term in the published Tanzanian material reviewed.

    Ministry of Women and Social Affairs (MoWSA), Ethiopia¶

    Federal executive ministry of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia responsible for social affairs, women and children affairs, and youth affairs; headed by a Minister with State Ministers for each of the three sectors Addis Ababa · Ethiopia national · Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia — executive ministry

    Social Work and Psychology Board of Namibia (Health Professions Councils of Namibia)¶

    Statutory professional board operating under the Health Professions Councils of Namibia (HPCNA); registers and regulates psychologists and social workers in Namibia; one of five HPCNA professional boards alongside the Allied Health Professions, Medical and Dental, Nursing and Pharmacy Boards Not publicly confirmed · Namibia national · Health Professions Councils of Namibia (HPCNA) — statutory regulator

    Legal Assistance Centre (LAC) — Gender Research and Advocacy Project, Namibia¶

    Namibian public-interest law organisation; operates a Gender Research & Advocacy Project (GRAP) with dedicated children's-law and family-law programmes covering the Children's Status Act, the Child Care and Protection Act, birth registration, corporal punishment and learner pregnancy Not publicly confirmed · Namibia national · Legal Assistance Centre (LAC), Namibia — public-interest law organisation

    Stance: LAC's own mission statement is that its staff "collectively strive to make the law accessible to those with the least access, through education, law reform, research, litigation, legal advice, representation and lobbying, with the ultimate aim of creating and maintaining a human rights culture in Namibia". Its Children's Status Act page states the Namibian position on post-separation contact directly: "Children born outside of marriage have a right to maintain contact with both parents. The parent without custody has an automatic right of reasonable access to the child unless a court decides that such access would be contrary to the child's best interests", adding that where parents cannot agree on a primary custodian "the court can decide". The same pages document the passage of the Child Care and Protection Act (passed March 2015, signed 22 April 2015, gazetted 29 May 2015, brought into force in 2019) and note that it repealed and absorbed the Children's Status Act. LAC does not use the term "parental alienation" on any page opened; it is listed as the documented Namibian institutional actor on children's contact and custody law rather than as a clinical service.

    Publications: - Taking care of children born outside of marriage (2004) — Legal Assistance Centre (Gender Research & Advocacy Project), Namibia — https://www.lac.org.na/index.php/projects/gender-research-advocacy-grap/children/childrens-status-act/ - Why children need fathers (2004) — Legal Assistance Centre (Gender Research & Advocacy Project), Namibia — https://www.lac.org.na/index.php/projects/gender-research-advocacy-grap/children/childrens-status-act/ - South African law on children born outside of marriage (2004) — Legal Assistance Centre (Gender Research & Advocacy Project), Namibia — https://www.lac.org.na/index.php/projects/gender-research-advocacy-grap/children/childrens-status-act/ - Does public opinion matter? (2006) — Legal Assistance Centre (Gender Research & Advocacy Project), Namibia — https://www.lac.org.na/index.php/projects/gender-research-advocacy-grap/children/childrens-status-act/ - A Family Affair — The Status of Cohabitation in Namibia (2010) — Legal Assistance Centre (Gender Research & Advocacy Project), Namibia — https://www.lac.org.na/index.php/projects/gender-research-advocacy-grap/family-law/ - Stepfamilies in Namibia (2011) — Legal Assistance Centre (Gender Research & Advocacy Project), Namibia — https://www.lac.org.na/index.php/projects/gender-research-advocacy-grap/family-law/

    Verification: - https://www.lac.org.na/ - https://www.lac.org.na/index.php/projects/gender-research-advocacy-grap/children/ - https://www.lac.org.na/index.php/projects/gender-research-advocacy-grap/children/childrens-status-act/ - https://www.lac.org.na/index.php/projects/gender-research-advocacy-grap/family-law/

Publication years are reproduced as displayed on those pages; two further family-law titles listed there without a year ("Namibian Law on Civil Marriage: A Question and Answer Guide" and "Inheritance Issues") are omitted because the schema requires an integer year. This is a public-interest law organisation, not a clinical or therapeutic provider, and is included on the same institutional basis as the existing legal and advocacy entries in this file (FIDA Kenya, WACOL, Project Alert).
